choices.feedback: Reduce the fraction! Dividing numerator and denominator of \(-\dfrac{6}{4}\) by \(2\) gives \(-\dfrac{3}{2}\), so the slopes are equal (and so are the \(y\)-intercepts).

choices.text: They are parallel lines \(9\) units apart vertically.
choices.feedback: Don't forget to divide \(12\) by \(4\)! Since \(\dfrac{12}{4} = 3\), both lines cross the \(y\)-axis at \(3\) and overlap completely.

questions.prompt: Blue Line A passes through \((-4, 4)\) and \((0, 1)\), and Green Line B passes through \((-3, -1)\) and \((3, -5)\). Do not just eyeball it — use their exact slopes! Are the two lines parallel?

choices.text: Yes; both lines have slope \(-\dfrac{3}{4}\) and different \(y\)-intercepts.
choices.feedback: Check Line B's slope carefully! \(m_B = \dfrac{-5 - (-1)}{3 - (-3)} = -\dfrac{2}{3}\), which is NOT equal to \(-\dfrac{3}{4}\).

choices.text: Yes; both lines have slope \(-\dfrac{2}{3}\) and never meet on the grid.
choices.feedback: Not meeting inside the visible grid does not prove lines are parallel! Compute Line A's slope: \(m_A = -\dfrac{3}{4} \neq -\dfrac{2}{3}\), so they intersect off-grid.

choices.text: No; Line A has slope \(-\dfrac{3}{4}\) and Line B has slope \(-\dfrac{2}{3}\), so they intersect.
choices.feedback: Even though they look close, check the exact slopes: \(m_A = \dfrac{1 - (4)}{0 - (-4)} = -\dfrac{3}{4}\) and \(m_B = \dfrac{-5 - (-1)}{3 - (-3)} = -\dfrac{2}{3}\). Because \(-\dfrac{3}{4} \neq -\dfrac{2}{3}\), the two lines are NOT parallel and will intersect.

choices.text: Yes; they look parallel on the graph and both slant in the same direction.
choices.feedback: Slanting in the same direction is not enough — parallel lines require EXACTLY equal slopes. Here \(m_A = -\dfrac{3}{4} \neq -\dfrac{2}{3} = m_B\).

questions.prompt: Compare Line P: \(y = 3 - \dfrac{2}{5}x\) and Line Q: \(y = -\dfrac{2}{5}x - 6\) on the same coordinate plane. Which statement is true?

choices.text: The lines are parallel, and Line P always lies \(9\) units below Line Q.
choices.feedback: You nailed the \(9\)-unit vertical gap, but check which \(y\)-intercept is greater! Since \(3 > -6\), Line P lies ABOVE Line Q.

choices.text: The lines are parallel, and Line P always lies \(3\) units above Line Q.
choices.feedback: Watch your integer subtraction! The \(y\)-intercepts are \(3\) and \(-6\), and the vertical distance between them is \(\lvert 3 - (-6) \rvert = 9\) units, not \(3\).

choices.text: The two lines are not parallel, so they intersect at one point.
choices.feedback: Reversed-order trap! In \(y = 3 - \dfrac{2}{5}x\), the slope is the coefficient of \(x\) (\(-\dfrac{2}{5}\)), not the constant \(3\). Both lines have \(m = -\dfrac{2}{5}\) and different \(y\)-intercepts, so they are parallel.

choices.text: The lines are parallel, and Line P always lies \(9\) units above Line Q.
choices.feedback: Rewrite Line P as \(y = -\dfrac{2}{5}x + 3\). Both lines have slope \(m = -\dfrac{2}{5}\), so they are parallel. Comparing \(y\)-intercepts: \(3 - (-6) = 9\), so Line P is always \(9\) units above Line Q.
